title: Wound care and drains
blurb: Assess wounds, spot infection, dress surgical wounds to NICE NG125 and manage drains, vacuum dressings and leg ulcers safely.
question: Mr Ibrahim, 63, had a laparotomy 5 days ago. His wound edges are red, swollen, hot and tender, with cloudy discharge, and his temperature is 38.2 °C. What does this suggest, and what should the nurse do?

teach.body: A wound heals by primary intention when its edges are brought together (sutures, clips, glue), and by secondary intention when it is left open to fill from the base with new tissue. Healing moves through overlapping phases: haemostasis (clotting), inflammation (cleaning up), proliferation (new tissue fills the gap) and maturation (scar strengthens over months). In plain English: closed wounds heal fast and neatly; open wounds take longer and need the right moist environment.

teach.caption: Timings overlap and vary with the person and the wound. Some redness and warmth early on is the normal inflammatory phase.

teach.h: Normal healing or surgical site infection?
teach.caption: NICE NG125: infection shows heat, redness, pain and swelling, and in more serious cases fever or raised white cells; it may cause edges to separate or an abscess. Check NEWS2 and think sepsis (NG253).

head: Point
Recommendation
rows: No topical antimicrobials to prevent infection
Interactive dressing; no Eusol and gauze
teach.caption: NICE NG125 recs 1.4.1–1.4.8. Ask a tissue viability nurse for advice on wounds healing by secondary intention.

teach.h: ANTT: protect key parts and key sites
teach.body: Aseptic non-touch technique protects the key parts (the parts of equipment that touch the wound or a sterile fluid, such as the inside of a dressing or a syringe tip) and the key site (the wound) from contamination. Hand hygiene, a clean field and never touching key parts are the core. Swab a wound only when it looks clinically infected; NICE CG179 advises against antibiotics based on a positive swab alone, and NICE NG15 asks for samples before antibiotics are started in hospital.
teach.cite: NICE NG125 rec 1.4.1; CG179; NG15 rec 1.1.27

teach.body: Spreading redness, swelling, heat, tenderness, cloudy discharge and fever point to a surgical site infection. The nurse calculates NEWS2 and considers sepsis, informs the surgical team promptly using SBAR, takes a wound swab as requested before antibiotics start, and redresses the wound using ANTT. She marks the edge of the redness, documents the wound's appearance and exudate, and reassesses regularly.

teach.h: Drains and vacuum dressings: what to watch

steps.label: Record output
steps.sub: Volume and type each check; chart the trend

steps.label: Look at it
steps.sub: Serous, blood-stained, fresh blood, bile, pus

steps.label: Vacuum dressing
steps.sub: Dressing stays collapsed; alarm = find and seal leak

steps.label: Secure
steps.sub: No kinks or traction; site checked

teach.caption: Follow the surgical plan for when a drain comes out. Never ignore a vacuum (negative pressure) alarm: a lost seal stops the therapy working.

items: Escalate red flags at once: acute infection, sepsis, limb-threatening ischaemia, suspected DVT, suspected skin cancer, bleeding varicose veins.
If there are no red flags, offer mild graduated compression (20 mmHg or less at the ankle) straight away, alongside a simple low-adherent dressing.
Complete a full assessment within 14 days, including arterial assessment with a Doppler ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI).
Strong compression (at least 40 mmHg at the ankle) only after that assessment.

teach.text: A positive wound swab is not the same as an infected wound: many wounds carry bacteria without infection. Treat the patient, not the swab. And strong compression must never go on before arterial assessment: compression on an ischaemic leg can cause serious harm.

items: Healing: haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, maturation; primary versus secondary intention.
Infection: heat, redness, pain, swelling, pus, separating edges, fever; check NEWS2 and escalate.
NG125: ANTT, sterile saline for 48 hours, shower after 48 hours, no topical antimicrobials on closed wounds.
Drains: record output and type; sudden fresh blood = escalate. Vacuum dressing alarm = find the leak.
Leg ulcers: red flags escalated, ABPI within 14 days before strong compression.

summary: You can now tell normal healing from surgical site infection, apply NICE NG125 rules for surgical wound care with ANTT, and monitor drains and vacuum dressings safely. You also know why arterial assessment comes before strong compression for leg ulcers.

A.q: Mrs Cole, 58, had a hip replacement yesterday. She asks when she can shower with her wound. What does NICE NG125 advise?
options: Once the sutures have been removed
After 48 hours from surgery
After 7 days if the wound is dry
After the first dressing change
A.why: NICE NG125 rec 1.4.3: advise patients that they may shower safely 48 hours after surgery.

whyNot.0: Waiting for suture removal is not required by NG125.
whyNot.2: 7 days is longer than NG125 advises.
whyNot.3: Showering is tied to 48 hours, not to the timing of dressing changes.

A.q: Which order lists the phases of wound healing correctly?
options: Inflammation, haemostasis, maturation, proliferation
Haemostasis, proliferation, inflammation, maturation
Proliferation, inflammation, haemostasis, maturation
Haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, maturation
A.why: Healing begins with haemostasis (clot), then inflammation, then proliferation (new tissue), then maturation (remodelling).

whyNot.2: Proliferation cannot happen before haemostasis and inflammation.

A.q: Mr Stone, 66, needs his surgical wound redressed. Which principle is central to aseptic non-touch technique?
options: Wearing sterile gloves for every dressing change
Cleaning the wound with an antiseptic each time
Protecting key parts and key sites from touch
Changing the dressing at least once every day
A.why: ANTT centres on protecting key parts and key sites from contamination; NG125 recommends ANTT for changing surgical dressings.

whyNot.0: Glove choice depends on the procedure; non-touch of key parts is the core principle.
whyNot.1: NG125 uses sterile saline for the first 48 hours and advises against topical antimicrobials on closed wounds.
whyNot.3: Daily changes are not required and disturb the wound unnecessarily.

B.q: Mr Ibrahim, 63, is 5 days after a laparotomy. His wound is red, hot, swollen and tender with cloudy discharge, and his temperature is 38.2 °C. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Apply a topical antiseptic and review at the next dressing change
Calculate NEWS2, inform the surgical team and swab as requested
Leave the dressing undisturbed for 48 hours to aid healing
Clean the wound with tap water and apply a dry gauze dressing
B.why: These are signs of surgical site infection (NG125). Assess the whole person with NEWS2, consider sepsis, escalate promptly and take a swab as requested before antibiotics (NG15).

whyNot.0: Topical antiseptics do not treat a surgical site infection and delay escalation.
whyNot.2: Leaving it ignores clear signs of infection and fever.
whyNot.3: This does not address the infection or the need to escalate.

B.q: Mr Price, 70, has a wound drain after hip surgery. It drained 40 mL in the first hour on the ward; in the last 30 minutes it has drained 350 mL of fresh blood. His pulse has risen. What should the nurse do?
options: Clamp the drain to stop the blood loss and recheck in an hour
Record the volume on the chart and empty the drain bottle
Escalate urgently as possible haemorrhage and assess ABCDE
Milk the drain tubing to check that there is no clot blocking it
B.why: A sudden large volume of fresh blood with a rising pulse suggests haemorrhage: assess ABCDE and escalate urgently.

whyNot.0: Clamping without instruction hides bleeding rather than stopping it.
whyNot.1: Recording alone delays urgent escalation of possible haemorrhage.
whyNot.3: The drain is clearly draining; the problem is the amount of blood.

B.q: Mrs Day, 82, has a sacral pressure ulcer. A routine swab grows Staphylococcus aureus. The ulcer shows no increase in pain, redness, heat or exudate and she is systemically well. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue current care without antibiotics
Request oral antibiotics to clear the organism
Apply a topical antibiotic cream to the wound
Repeat the swab daily until it is negative
B.why: NICE CG179: do not offer systemic antibiotics based only on positive wound cultures without clinical evidence of infection.

whyNot.1: Antibiotics for colonisation without infection go against CG179 and antimicrobial stewardship.
whyNot.2: Topical antimicrobials are not routinely used on pressure ulcers.
whyNot.3: Repeated swabbing of a wound with no clinical infection does not change management.

C.q: Mr Hart, 74, has a venous leg ulcer and visits the community nurse. He has no red flag signs and is at low risk of pressure damage. His ABPI has not yet been measured. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Apply strong compression at 40 mmHg today and measure ABPI later
Hold compression until a vascular surgeon has reviewed him
Apply a simple dressing and review the ulcer in three months
Apply mild compression now and complete ABPI within 14 days
C.why: NWCSP Leg Ulcer Recommendations (2023): offer mild graduated compression (20 mmHg or less) as immediate care if no red flags, and complete a comprehensive assessment including ABPI within 14 days before strong compression.

whyNot.0: Strong compression needs arterial assessment first.
whyNot.1: Mild compression is recommended now; a surgical review is not needed first without red flags.
whyNot.2: Waiting three months delays healing; assessment is due within 14 days.

C.q: Ms Green, 49, has negative pressure wound therapy on a leg wound. The pump alarms for a leak and the foam is no longer collapsed. What should the nurse do first?
options: Switch the pump off and leave it until the next planned change
Turn the pressure setting up to overcome the leak
Find and seal the leak, then check the foam collapses
Remove the whole dressing and pack the wound with dry gauze
C.why: Therapy only works with an airtight seal; locate the leak, seal it (per manufacturer's guidance) and check the foam collapses. If the seal cannot be restored, follow local policy for replacing the dressing.

whyNot.0: Leaving it off stops the therapy and can trap exudate in the foam.
whyNot.1: Changing the prescribed pressure does not fix a leak.
whyNot.3: Removing the dressing is not the first step when a leak can be sealed.

C.q: Mr Ali, 55, has a surgical wound that separated on day 4 and was opened to drain pus. It is now day 6 and he is going home with the wound healing by secondary intention. Which advice fits NICE NG125?
options: Clean with tap water and use an interactive dressing
Use sterile saline and apply moist cotton gauze each day
Apply an antiseptic solution such as Eusol with gauze packing
Avoid getting the wound wet until it has fully closed over
C.why: NG125: after 48 hours tap water can be used if a wound has separated or been opened to drain pus; use an interactive dressing for secondary intention healing and avoid Eusol and gauze or moist cotton gauze.

whyNot.1: Moist cotton gauze is advised against for wounds healing by secondary intention.
whyNot.2: NG125 advises against Eusol and gauze.
whyNot.3: Showering is safe after 48 hours; avoiding water is not required.

reteach.title: Read the wound, then the person
reteach.question: A wound is a window into how someone is recovering. What do you look at, and what makes you worried?

blocks.body: First the wound: size, bed, exudate (amount, colour, smell), edges and the skin around it. Then the person: temperature, NEWS2, pain, nutrition and mobility. A wound that is getting redder, hotter, more painful and more productive, in a person whose observations are changing, is an infection until proven otherwise and needs escalating.

blocks.text: Volume matters as much as colour: a small, falling volume of blood-stained fluid is usually fine; a sudden rise in fresh blood is not.

explain.body: Primary intention: edges brought together. Secondary intention: left open to heal from the base. Phases: haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, maturation.

test.q: A wound left open to fill from the base is healing by which route?
options: Primary intention
Tertiary closure
Secondary intention
Delayed wound suturing
test.why: Secondary intention describes healing from the base of an open wound.

whyNot.0: Primary intention means edges are brought together.
whyNot.1: Tertiary (delayed primary) closure is a later surgical closure, not open healing.
whyNot.3: Delayed suturing closes the wound later; it is not healing from the base.

explain.body: ANTT for dressing changes. Sterile saline for cleansing up to 48 hours. Showering safe after 48 hours. Tap water after 48 hours if the wound has separated or been opened. No topical antimicrobials on wounds healing by primary intention.

test.q: What should be used to cleanse a surgical wound in the first 48 hours?
options: Tap water
Sterile saline
Povidone-iodine
Chlorhexidine
test.why: NICE NG125 rec 1.4.2: use sterile saline for wound cleansing up to 48 hours after surgery.

whyNot.0: Tap water is for after 48 hours if the wound has separated or been opened.
whyNot.2: Topical antimicrobials are not advised for closed surgical wounds.
whyNot.3: Chlorhexidine is a skin prep before incision, not routine wound cleansing.

explain.body: Heat, redness, pain, swelling, pus, separating edges; in serious cases fever and raised white cells. Check NEWS2, consider sepsis, escalate, swab before antibiotics if requested. Do not treat a positive swab alone.

test.q: Which finding most strongly suggests a surgical wound is infected?
options: A small amount of clear fluid
Increasing redness, heat and pus
Mild itching around the edges
Slight bruising near the incision
test.why: NG125 describes infection as heat, redness, pain and swelling, with pus or separating edges.

whyNot.0: Small clear exudate is expected in healing.
whyNot.2: Itching is common as wounds heal.
whyNot.3: Mild bruising is common after surgery.

explain.body: Escalate red flags. If none, mild compression (20 mmHg or less) can start at once. Comprehensive assessment with Doppler ABPI within 14 days before strong compression (at least 40 mmHg).

test.q: Within what time does the NWCSP recommend a full leg ulcer assessment including ABPI?
options: 14 days
48 hours
28 days
3 months
test.why: NWCSP Leg Ulcer Recommendations: comprehensive assessment within 14 days.

whyNot.1: 48 hours is not the NWCSP standard for this assessment.
whyNot.2: 28 days is double the recommended window.
whyNot.3: 3 months would leave the ulcer untreated far too long.
